# Check catalog

All 106 checks OpenScore can report, grouped by factor, generated from the knowledge base (`openscore/kb.py`). The severity is the default; a few checks adjust it from what they find (for example, certificate expiry gets more severe as the date gets closer). Findings matched only on a version banner are reported as *tentative*.

In the verify commands, `{asset}` is the host or IP, `{domain}` the domain you scanned and `{url}` the URL in the evidence; the report fills them in.

Third-party results (nuclei templates, testssl.sh rows) use the generic `nuclei_finding` and `tls_testssl` entries, with the tool's own title.

| Factor | Weight | Checks |
|---|---|---|
| [Network Security](#network) | 1.0 | 13 |
| [Patching Cadence](#patching) | 1.0 | 8 |
| [Information Exposure](#exposure) | 1.0 | 19 |
| [IP & Domain Reputation](#reputation) | 0.9 | 6 |

| [DNS Health](#dns) | 0.6 | 10 |

<a id="network"></a>

## Network Security

Risky services reachable from the internet (RDP, SMB, databases, remote admin).

### Unauthenticated-by-default datastore exposed

`net_exposed_datastore` · default severity **critical**

**Why it matters:** Redis, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Memcached, CouchDB etc. are routinely wiped/ransomed when exposed.

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -sV -p <port> {asset}`. For Redis: `redis-cli -h {asset} ping` returning PONG = no auth (only do this with authorization).

**How to fix:** Firewall immediately, enable authentication, bind to localhost/private IPs.


### Docker / Kubernetes API exposed

`net_exposed_docker` · default severity **critical**

**Why it matters:** An exposed container API usually means full host compromise.

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -sV -p <port> {asset}`.

**How to fix:** Firewall the port; require TLS client auth; never expose 2375.


### SMB / NetBIOS / RPC exposed

`net_exposed_smb` · default severity **critical**

**Why it matters:** SMB (445/139) and RPC (135) should never be internet-reachable (EternalBlue, relay attacks).

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -p 135,139,445 {asset}`. 'filtered' is NOT open. Many ISPs block 445 outbound — test from a cloud VM if your network blocks it.

**How to fix:** Block TCP 135/137-139/445 inbound at the perimeter.


### Database port exposed

`net_exposed_db` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL or Oracle reachable from the internet.

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -sV -p <port> {asset}`.

**How to fix:** Bind to private interfaces / firewall to application servers only; never expose DBs publicly.


### LDAP / Active Directory service exposed

`net_exposed_ldap` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** Domain controllers or LDAP directories should not be internet-reachable.

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -sV -p 389,636,3268,88 {asset}`.

**How to fix:** Block 389/636/3268/88 inbound; use Entra ID for external auth.


### RDP exposed to the internet

`net_exposed_rdp` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** Internet-facing RDP is brute-forced constantly and is a leading ransomware entry point.

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -p 3389 {asset}` (PowerShell: `Test-NetConnection {asset} -Port 3389`). If the finding came only from Shodan and your live scan shows closed, the data is stale.

**How to fix:** Close 3389 at the firewall. Use a VPN with MFA, Azure Bastion, Entra ID App Proxy / RD Gateway with MFA instead.


### Remote administration service exposed

`net_exposed_remote_admin` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** VNC, WinRM, Webmin, SNMP or similar admin interfaces reachable from the internet.

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -sV -p <port> {asset}`.

**How to fix:** Restrict to VPN / management network; require MFA.


### Telnet exposed

`net_exposed_telnet` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** Cleartext remote login, frequently with default credentials on network gear.

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -sV -p 23 {asset}`.

**How to fix:** Disable Telnet; use SSH restricted by source IP.


### Management web interface exposed

`net_exposed_admin_web` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Firewall/router/hypervisor management UI (e.g. 8443/10443/4443, Webmin, Kibana) reachable publicly.

**How to verify:** Browse to https://{asset}:&lt;port> — identify what the login page is.

**How to fix:** Move management interfaces to an internal VLAN or restrict by source IP.


### FTP exposed

`net_exposed_ftp` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** FTP sends credentials in cleartext.

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -sV -p 21 {asset}`.

**How to fix:** Replace with SFTP/FTPS or a file-sharing service.


### Cleartext mail protocol exposed (POP3/IMAP)

`net_exposed_cleartext_mail` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** POP3/IMAP without TLS exposes credentials.

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -sV -p 110,143 {asset}`.

**How to fix:** Disable 110/143; use 995/993 only, or disable legacy protocols entirely (M365: turn off POP/IMAP per mailbox and block legacy auth via Conditional Access).


### Additional open port

`net_exposed_other` · default severity **info**

**Why it matters:** Open port not in the high-risk list; confirm it is intentional.

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -sV -p <port> {asset}`.

**How to fix:** Close any service that doesn't need to be internet-facing.


### SSH exposed

`net_exposed_ssh` · default severity **info**

**Why it matters:** Generally acceptable if key-only auth and patched, but reduces attack surface to restrict it.

**How to verify:** `nmap -Pn -sV -p 22 {asset}`.

**How to fix:** Disable password auth, restrict source IPs, keep OpenSSH patched.


<a id="patching"></a>

## Patching Cadence

End-of-life or outdated software and known-vulnerable versions (CISA KEV / EPSS).

### Known Exploited Vulnerability (CISA KEV)

`vuln_kev` · default severity **critical**

**Why it matters:** This CVE is actively exploited in the wild and is on CISA's KEV catalog. Detection is version-based, so verify, but treat as urgent.

**How to verify:** Version-based match. Confirm the installed version/build on the device itself and compare to the vendor advisory's fixed version. Treat as urgent until disproven.

**How to fix:** Patch immediately per the vendor advisory; if you can't, remove internet exposure and hunt for signs of compromise.

**References:** <https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog>

### End-of-life software detected

`sw_eol` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** This product version no longer receives security updates from the vendor.

**How to verify:** Check the banner: `curl -sI {url} \| grep -iE 'server\|x-powered'`. COMMON FALSE POSITIVE: Linux distros (RHEL, Ubuntu, Debian) backport security fixes without changing the version string — check the OS release with the server owner (`apache2 -v`, `rpm -q httpd`, `dpkg -l \| grep apache2`).

**How to fix:** Upgrade to a supported release. If the banner is wrong (e.g. backported OS packages), suppress the version banner so scanners stop flagging it.

**References:** <https://endoflife.date/>

### Vulnerability with high exploit probability (EPSS)

`vuln_high_epss` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** FIRST EPSS estimates a high probability this CVE is exploited in the next 30 days.

**How to verify:** Version-based match. Confirm installed version against the CVE's affected range on nvd.nist.gov.

**How to fix:** Prioritise patching; verify version and apply vendor fix.

**References:** <https://www.first.org/epss/>

### Remote-access/VPN appliance exposed

`edge_appliance_exposed` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** VPN and gateway appliances (Fortinet, Ivanti/Pulse, Citrix, Palo Alto, SonicWall) are the #1 initial-access vector for ransomware. Exposure is expected, but they must be patched within days of advisories.

**How to verify:** Browse to the URL in the evidence. Then log in to the appliance and compare firmware to the vendor PSIRT / CISA KEV entries.

**How to fix:** Confirm firmware is current, subscribe to the vendor PSIRT feed, require MFA, and check CISA KEV for this product.


### On-premises Exchange (OWA/ECP) exposed

`exchange_onprem_exposed` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** On-prem Exchange has repeatedly been mass-exploited (ProxyLogon, ProxyShell). The build number below can be checked against Microsoft's build list.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI https://{asset}/owa/auth/logon.aspx \| grep -i x-owa-version`, then look the build up in Microsoft's Exchange build numbers table.

**How to fix:** Apply the latest Exchange CU + SU, restrict /ecp to internal networks, or decommission if mailboxes are already in Exchange Online.

**References:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/exchange/new-features/build-numbers-and-release-dates>

### Software not on latest patch release

`sw_outdated` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** A newer patch release exists in this supported branch.

**How to verify:** Same as above — on distro packages, compare against the distro's security tracker (ubuntu.com/security, access.redhat.com), not upstream.

**How to fix:** Apply the latest vendor patch for this branch.


### Potential CVE based on detected version

`vuln_cve` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Version-based match from Shodan InternetDB/nuclei; not exploit-verified.

**How to verify:** Version-based match from Shodan's fingerprint (may be days–weeks old). Confirm installed version and whether the vulnerable component/feature is enabled.

**How to fix:** Confirm the installed version and apply vendor patches.


### Detected software is supported

`sw_supported` · passed check (no deduction)


<a id="exposure"></a>

## Information Exposure

Leaked files, debug pages, version banners and breached accounts.

### Exposed cloud credentials file

`exp_aws_creds` · default severity **critical**

**Why it matters:** AWS credentials readable over HTTP.

**How to verify:** Request the URL in the evidence; confirm `aws_access_key_id`.

**How to fix:** Deactivate the keys in IAM immediately, then remove the file.


### Exposed configuration/backup file

`exp_config_backup` · default severity **critical**

**Why it matters:** Configuration file (wp-config, web.config, etc.) readable, likely with credentials.

**How to verify:** Request the URL in the evidence and confirm it contains configuration, not a 'not found' page.

**How to fix:** Delete the file from the web root and rotate credentials.


### Exposed .env file with secrets

`exp_env` · default severity **critical**

**Why it matters:** Environment file containing credentials/API keys is publicly readable.

**How to verify:** `curl -s {url} \| head -3` — confirm it contains real KEY=value lines (don't store the output).

**How to fix:** Remove from web root, block dotfiles, and rotate every secret in it NOW.


### Exposed .git repository

`exp_git` · default severity **critical**

**Why it matters:** Source code and history (often including secrets) can be downloaded.

**How to verify:** `curl -s {url}` returns `ref: refs/heads/...`.

**How to fix:** Block access to /.git/ at the web server and rotate any secrets in the repo history.


### Spring Boot Actuator endpoint exposed

`exp_actuator` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** /actuator/env etc. leaks configuration and sometimes allows RCE.

**How to verify:** `curl -s {url} \| head -c 300`.

**How to fix:** Set management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health and secure the rest.


### Downloadable backup archive / SQL dump

`exp_backup_archive` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** Backup archives or database dumps in the web root.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI <url>` — Content-Length and Content-Type (application/zip, application/sql) confirm.

**How to fix:** Remove from the web root; store backups outside public paths.


### Admin panel publicly reachable

`exp_admin_panel` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Database/admin UI (e.g. phpMyAdmin) reachable from the internet.

**How to verify:** Browse to the URL in the evidence — confirm it's a real login page and not a honeypot/WAF block page.

**How to fix:** Restrict by IP / VPN, or remove.


### ASP.NET debug handler exposed

`exp_debug_handler` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** elmah.axd / trace.axd reveal errors, requests, and sometimes session cookies.

**How to verify:** Browse to the URL in the evidence.

**How to fix:** Remove the handler or restrict to localhost in web.config.


### phpinfo() page exposed

`exp_phpinfo` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Reveals PHP/OS versions, paths, environment variables.

**How to verify:** Browse to the URL in the evidence.

**How to fix:** Delete phpinfo/info.php from the server.


### Apache server-status exposed

`exp_server_status` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Reveals client IPs, URLs being requested and internal vhosts.

**How to verify:** Browse to {url}.

**How to fix:** Restrict /server-status to localhost (`Require local`).


### Exposed .svn metadata

`exp_svn` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Subversion metadata reveals source files.

**How to verify:** `curl -s {url}`.

**How to fix:** Block /.svn/ and remove it from the web root.


### Directory listing enabled

`http_dir_listing` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Web server lists directory contents, exposing files not meant to be linked.

**How to verify:** Open the URL in the evidence — an 'Index of /' page confirms.

**How to fix:** Disable autoindex (Nginx `autoindex off;`, Apache `Options -Indexes`, IIS Directory Browsing off).


### Accounts found in public breaches (HIBP)

`leak_breached_accounts` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Email addresses on this domain appear in known data breaches; reused passwords enable credential stuffing.

**How to verify:** Review the HIBP domain dashboard. Old breaches of since-departed users are lower risk; check whether affected users still exist in Entra ID.

**How to fix:** Force password resets for affected users, enforce MFA (Entra Conditional Access), and enable Entra ID Password Protection / leaked-credential detection.

**References:** <https://haveibeenpwned.com/DomainSearch>

### Permissive crossdomain.xml

`exp_crossdomain` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** Allows any domain (`*`) to make cross-domain Flash/Silverlight requests.

**How to verify:** `curl -s {url}`.

**How to fix:** Remove the file or restrict domains.


### Exposed .DS_Store

`exp_ds_store` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** macOS metadata file lists directory contents.

**How to verify:** `curl -s {url} \| xxd \| head -1` shows `Bud1`.

**How to fix:** Delete .DS_Store files and block dotfiles.


### Software version disclosed in banner/header

`exp_version_disclosure` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** Exact version numbers let attackers and automated scanners match you to CVEs instantly.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI {url} \| grep -iE 'server\|x-powered\|x-aspnet'`.

**How to fix:** IIS: remove Server header (`removeServerHeader="true"` in requestFiltering) and X-Powered-By / X-AspNet-Version. Nginx: `server_tokens off;`. Apache: `ServerTokens Prod` + `ServerSignature Off`. PHP: `expose_php = Off`.


### WordPress user enumeration via REST API

`exp_wp_user_enum` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** Usernames are listed at /wp-json/wp/v2/users, aiding password attacks.

**How to verify:** `curl -s {url}` lists usernames.

**How to fix:** Restrict the users endpoint (security plugin or a small mu-plugin).


### WordPress xmlrpc.php enabled

`exp_xmlrpc` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** Used for credential brute-force amplification and pingback DDoS.

**How to verify:** `curl -s {url}`.

**How to fix:** Disable XML-RPC unless Jetpack/mobile app needs it.


### API documentation publicly accessible

`exp_api_docs` · default severity **info**

**Why it matters:** Swagger/OpenAPI docs map the attack surface; fine if intended.

**How to verify:** Browse to the URL in the evidence; decide whether the API is meant to be public.

**How to fix:** Restrict if the API is not meant to be public.


<a id="reputation"></a>

## IP & Domain Reputation

Blocklist listings, abuse reports and signs of compromised hosts.

### IP listed on a spam/abuse blocklist

`rep_dnsbl_listed` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** Blocklisted IPs often indicate a compromised host, open relay, or infected device sending spam.

**How to verify:** Look the IP up at check.spamhaus.org / mxtoolbox.com/blacklists. If the IP is shared hosting/cloud, the listing may belong to a previous or neighboring tenant.

**How to fix:** Identify what on that IP is sending mail/traffic, clean it, then request delisting via the blocklist's lookup page.

**References:** <https://check.spamhaus.org/>

### Domain on a blocklist

`rep_domain_blocklisted` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** The domain appears on a domain blocklist (malware/phishing/spam).

**How to verify:** Check the domain at check.spamhaus.org and surbl.org/surbl-analysis.

**How to fix:** Check for compromised web content or abused redirects, clean up, then request removal.


### IP observed scanning/attacking the internet (GreyNoise)

`rep_greynoise_malicious` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** GreyNoise sensors saw this IP performing malicious internet-wide activity — usually a compromised host.

**How to verify:** Open https://viz.greynoise.io/ip/{asset}.

**How to fix:** Treat as an incident: isolate the host behind that IP and investigate.

**References:** <https://viz.greynoise.io/>

### Shodan tags this IP as compromised/malware

`rep_shodan_tag` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** Shodan has tagged the host (e.g. 'compromised', 'malware', 'c2', 'doublepulsar').

**How to verify:** Open https://www.shodan.io/host/{asset}.

**How to fix:** Treat as an incident and investigate the host.


### IP reported for abuse (AbuseIPDB)

`rep_abuseipdb` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Other organizations have reported malicious traffic from this IP.

**How to verify:** Open https://www.abuseipdb.com/check/{asset} — read the report categories and dates. Old reports on a recently-acquired cloud IP are a false positive for the current owner.

**How to fix:** Investigate the host for compromise (malware, brute-forcing outbound, proxies). Shared/cloud IPs may carry reports from previous tenants; if so, request delisting with the reporting service.

**References:** <https://www.abuseipdb.com/>

### No reputation issues found

`rep_clean` · passed check (no deduction)


<a id="appsec"></a>

## Application Security

HTTP security headers, cookie flags, HTTPS redirects, CORS.

### CORS reflects arbitrary Origin with credentials

`http_cors_reflect` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** Any website can make authenticated requests and read responses on behalf of logged-in users.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI -H 'Origin: https://evil.example' {url}` — both `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` confirm. Only exploitable if the endpoint returns user-specific data.

**How to fix:** Only echo origins from an allow-list; never combine a reflected origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.


### Cookie set without Secure flag

`http_cookie_insecure` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Cookie can be sent over plain HTTP and intercepted.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI {url} \| grep -i set-cookie` — check for `Secure`. Load-balancer stickiness cookies are common, low-impact offenders.

**How to fix:** Set the Secure attribute on all cookies served over HTTPS.


### HSTS header missing

`http_hsts_missing` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Without Strict-Transport-Security a network attacker can downgrade users to HTTP (SSL stripping).

**How to verify:** `curl -sI {url} \| grep -i strict-transport` (PowerShell: `curl.exe -sI https://{asset}`). If the site sits behind a CDN/WAF, check the CDN's HSTS setting too.

**How to fix:** Add `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` on HTTPS responses.

**References:** <https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Strict-Transport-Security>

### HTTP does not redirect to HTTPS

`http_no_redirect` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Visitors who type the bare domain get an unencrypted page.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI {url}` — expect `301/308` with `Location: https://...`.

**How to fix:** Return a 301 from http:// to https:// for all paths. IIS: URL Rewrite rule; Nginx: `return 301 https://$host$request_uri;`.


### Nuclei template match

`nuclei_finding` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** See evidence for template details.

**How to verify:** Re-run the single template: `nuclei -u https://{asset} -id {template} -debug` and inspect the matched request/response.

**How to fix:** See the template references in the evidence.


### Session-like cookie without HttpOnly

`http_cookie_httponly` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** JavaScript (and therefore XSS) can read the cookie.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI {url} \| grep -i set-cookie` — check for `HttpOnly`. Cookies that front-end JS must read (e.g. CSRF tokens) legitimately omit it → mark false positive.

**How to fix:** Set HttpOnly on session/auth cookies.


### Content-Security-Policy header missing

`http_csp_missing` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** CSP limits where scripts can load from and is the main browser-side defense against XSS.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI {url} \| grep -i content-security`. Some apps set CSP only via &lt;meta> tag — check page source; meta CSP still counts for XSS but not for frame-ancestors.

**How to fix:** Start with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` to learn, then enforce. Minimum useful: `default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'`.

**References:** <https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/CSP>

### HSTS max-age shorter than 180 days

`http_hsts_short` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** Short HSTS lifetimes give weak protection.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI {url} \| grep -i strict-transport` — check max-age.

**How to fix:** Use max-age=31536000 (1 year).


### Mixed content on HTTPS page

`http_mixed_content` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** HTTPS page loads scripts/styles over HTTP, which can be tampered with.

**How to verify:** Open https://{asset} in a browser → DevTools Console shows 'Mixed Content' warnings.

**How to fix:** Load all resources over https:// (or protocol-relative / same-origin).


### X-Content-Type-Options header missing

`http_xcto_missing` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** Browsers may MIME-sniff responses into executable types.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI {url} \| grep -i x-content-type`.

**How to fix:** Add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.


### Clickjacking protection missing

`http_xfo_missing` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** Neither X-Frame-Options nor CSP frame-ancestors is set, so the site can be framed.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI {url} \| grep -iE 'x-frame\|frame-ancestors'`.

**How to fix:** Add `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` or CSP `frame-ancestors 'self'`.


### Cookie without SameSite attribute

`http_cookie_samesite` · default severity **info**

**Why it matters:** Browsers default to Lax, but explicit SameSite hardens against CSRF.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI {url} \| grep -i set-cookie`.

**How to fix:** Set `SameSite=Lax` (or Strict) explicitly.


### CORS allows any origin (*)

`http_cors_wildcard` · default severity **info**

**Why it matters:** Fine for truly public content; a problem if responses contain private data.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI -H 'Origin: https://x.example' https://{asset}`.

**How to fix:** Restrict Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the origins that need it.


### Referrer-Policy header missing

`http_referrer_missing` · default severity **info**

**Why it matters:** Full URLs (possibly with tokens) may leak to third parties via Referer.

**How to verify:** `curl -sI {url} \| grep -i referrer-policy`.

**How to fix:** Add `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`.


### No security.txt

`http_security_txt_missing` · default severity **info**

**Why it matters:** security.txt tells researchers how to report vulnerabilities to you.

**How to verify:** `curl -s https://{domain}/.well-known/security.txt`.

**How to fix:** Publish /.well-known/security.txt with Contact: and Expires: fields (securitytxt.org).

**References:** <https://securitytxt.org/>

### Core security headers present

`http_headers_ok` · passed check (no deduction)


<a id="tls"></a>

## TLS / Certificates

Certificate validity, protocol versions, key strength.

### TLS certificate expired

`tls_cert_expired` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** Browsers show a full-page warning; users learn to click through warnings.

**How to verify:** `echo \| openssl s_client -connect {asset}:443 -servername {asset} 2>/dev/null \| openssl x509 -noout -dates`.

**How to fix:** Renew the certificate and automate renewal (ACME / certbot / host auto-renew).


### TLS certificate does not match hostname

`tls_cert_hostname_mismatch` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** The certificate is valid for other names, so browsers will warn.

**How to verify:** `echo \| openssl s_client -connect {asset}:443 -servername {asset} 2>/dev/null \| openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectAltName`.

**How to fix:** Issue a certificate whose SAN includes this hostname, or remove the DNS record if the host is unused.


### TLS certificate not trusted (self-signed / incomplete chain)

`tls_cert_untrusted` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** The certificate does not chain to a public root, or intermediates are missing.

**How to verify:** `curl -vI https://{asset}` — 'unable to get local issuer' = missing intermediate; also SSL Labs. Note: corporate TLS-inspection proxies on YOUR side can cause this — re-test from another network.

**How to fix:** Use a publicly trusted certificate and configure the full chain (server cert + intermediates) on the server.


### SSLv2/SSLv3 enabled

`tls_sslv3` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** Broken protocols (POODLE, DROWN).

**How to verify:** `nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 {asset}` or `testssl.sh -p {asset}`.

**How to fix:** Disable SSLv2/SSLv3 entirely.


### TLS certificate expires soon

`tls_cert_expiring` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Certificate expires within 30 days (high within 7 days, medium within 14, low otherwise).

**How to verify:** `echo \| openssl s_client -connect {asset}:443 -servername {asset} 2>/dev/null \| openssl x509 -noout -enddate`.

**How to fix:** Renew now and put certificate expiry on monitoring.


### Website not available over HTTPS

`tls_no_https` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** The site serves HTTP only; traffic and credentials travel in cleartext.

**How to verify:** `curl -vI https://{asset}` — connection refused/timeout confirms.

**How to fix:** Install a certificate (free via Let's Encrypt / your host / Cloudflare) and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.


### Legacy TLS 1.0 / 1.1 enabled

`tls_old_protocol` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated (RFC 8996) and fail PCI DSS.

**How to verify:** `openssl s_client -connect {asset}:443 -tls1_1` (or `nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 {asset}`). Note: on OpenSSL 3 add `-cipher 'DEFAULT:@SECLEVEL=0'` or the local client refuses first.

**How to fix:** Disable TLS 1.0/1.1; allow TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only. IIS: use IIS Crypto or the SCHANNEL registry keys. Nginx: `ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;`. Apache: `SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3`.

**References:** <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996>

### Certificate signed with SHA-1/MD5

`tls_sha1_sig` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Deprecated signature algorithm.

**How to verify:** `... \| openssl x509 -noout -text \| grep 'Signature Algorithm'`.

**How to fix:** Reissue with SHA-256.


### TLS issue reported by testssl.sh

`tls_testssl` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** See evidence for the specific testssl.sh finding.

**How to verify:** `testssl.sh {asset}` and read the matching item.

**How to fix:** See https://testssl.sh and the Mozilla TLS guidelines for the specific item.


### Weak cipher suites accepted

`tls_weak_cipher` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Server accepts obsolete ciphers (RC4, 3DES, NULL, EXPORT, or non-forward-secret).

**How to verify:** `nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 {asset}` — look for grades below A, or run testssl.sh.

**How to fix:** Use the Mozilla 'intermediate' cipher configuration (ssl-config.mozilla.org).

**References:** <https://ssl-config.mozilla.org/>

### Weak certificate key (RSA < 2048 bits)

`tls_weak_key` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Short RSA keys are considered breakable.

**How to verify:** `echo \| openssl s_client -connect {asset}:443 -servername {asset} 2>/dev/null \| openssl x509 -noout -text \| grep 'Public-Key'`.

**How to fix:** Reissue with RSA 2048+ or ECDSA P-256.


### TLS 1.3 not supported

`tls_no_tls13` · default severity **info**

**Why it matters:** Not a vulnerability, but TLS 1.3 is faster and removes legacy crypto.

**How to verify:** `openssl s_client -connect {asset}:443 -tls1_3`.

**How to fix:** Enable TLS 1.3 (Windows Server 2022+, OpenSSL 1.1.1+).


### TLS certificate valid and trusted

`tls_ok` · passed check (no deduction)


<a id="email"></a>

## Email Security

SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MTA-STS — spoofing and phishing resistance.

### No DMARC record

`email_dmarc_missing` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** DMARC tells receivers what to do when SPF/DKIM fail and sends you reports. Without it, spoofed mail claiming to be from this domain is usually delivered.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT _dmarc.{domain}` (Windows: `nslookup -type=txt _dmarc.{domain}`).

**How to fix:** Start in monitoring: TXT `_dmarc.<domain>` = `v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@<domain>; fo=1`. Review reports for 2–4 weeks, then move to `p=quarantine` and finally `p=reject`.

**References:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/email-authentication-dmarc-configure>

### No SPF record

`email_spf_missing` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** Without SPF, receiving mail servers cannot tell which servers may send mail for this domain, which makes spoofing it trivial.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT {domain}` (Windows: `nslookup -type=txt {domain}`) — look for a line starting v=spf1. Query an authoritative NS (`dig @ns1.provider TXT {domain}`) to rule out resolver caching.

**How to fix:** Publish one TXT record at the domain apex. M365 only: `v=spf1 include:spf.protection.outlook.com -all`. Add includes for every other sender (marketing, CRM, ticketing). If the domain never sends mail: `v=spf1 -all`.

**References:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/email-authentication-spf-configure>

### Multiple SPF records (SPF permerror)

`email_spf_multiple` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** RFC 7208 allows exactly one v=spf1 record. With two or more, receivers treat SPF as a permanent error and it provides no protection.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT {domain} \| grep -i spf1` — more than one line = permerror.

**How to fix:** Merge all mechanisms into a single `v=spf1 ... -all` TXT record and delete the rest.

**References:** <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208#section-4.5>

### SPF allows any sender (+all / ?all)

`email_spf_permissive` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** `+all` authorizes every server on the internet; `?all` is neutral. Either defeats SPF.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT {domain}` — check the final `all` qualifier.

**How to fix:** End the record with `-all` (hard fail) or at minimum `~all` while DMARC is in monitoring.


### DKIM key shorter than 2048 bits

`email_dkim_weak_key` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** 1024-bit RSA DKIM keys are considered weak; anything shorter is breakable.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT <selector>._domainkey.{domain}` and decode the p= key length (`echo <p> \| base64 -d \| openssl rsa -pubin -inform DER -text -noout \| head -1`).

**How to fix:** Rotate to 2048-bit keys. M365: Rotate-DkimSigningConfig -KeySize 2048 -Identity &lt;domain>


### DMARC record is malformed

`email_dmarc_invalid` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** Receivers ignore DMARC records that don't start with v=DMARC1 and contain a valid p= tag, or when more than one record exists.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT _dmarc.{domain}` — check for multiple records or a missing/invalid p= tag.

**How to fix:** Publish exactly one record: `v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:...`.


### DMARC policy is p=none (monitor only)

`email_dmarc_none` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** p=none collects reports but does not stop spoofed mail.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT _dmarc.{domain}` — shows p=none.

**How to fix:** After confirming legitimate senders pass SPF/DKIM in the aggregate reports, raise to `p=quarantine` then `p=reject`.


### SPF exceeds 10 DNS lookups

`email_spf_too_many_lookups` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** SPF evaluation is limited to 10 DNS-querying mechanisms (include, a, mx, ptr, exists, redirect). Beyond that receivers return permerror and SPF fails.

**How to verify:** Paste the domain into an SPF lookup counter (e.g. MXToolbox SPF, dmarcian SPF surveyor) — it should report >10 lookups.

**How to fix:** Remove unused includes, replace `a`/`mx` with ip4/ip6 ranges, or move bulk senders to a subdomain (e.g. mail.example.com) with its own SPF.

**References:** <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208#section-4.6.4>

### No DKIM key found at common selectors

`email_dkim_not_found` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** DKIM selectors can't be enumerated, so this is tentative. We checked common selectors (including Microsoft 365's selector1/selector2) and found none.

**How to verify:** LIKELY FALSE POSITIVE if the org uses a custom selector. Open the headers of any email sent from {domain} and read `DKIM-Signature: ... s=<selector>`; then `dig +short TXT <selector>._domainkey.{domain}`. Re-run with `--dkim-selectors <selector>`.

**How to fix:** Microsoft 365: Defender portal → Email & collaboration → Policies → Threat policies → Email authentication settings → DKIM → select the domain → publish the two CNAMEs shown (selector1._domainkey / selector2._domainkey → *.onmicrosoft.com) → toggle 'Sign messages for this domain with DKIM signatures' ON. PowerShell: New-DkimSigningConfig -DomainName &lt;domain> -Enabled $true For other senders, enable DKIM in that platform and publish its key.

**References:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/email-authentication-dkim-configure>

### DMARC has no aggregate report address (rua)

`email_dmarc_no_rua` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** Without rua you get no visibility into who is sending as your domain.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT _dmarc.{domain}` — no rua= tag.

**How to fix:** Add `rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@<domain>` (or a free/paid DMARC report processor).


### DMARC enforcement applies to only part of the mail (pct<100)

`email_dmarc_partial` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** With pct below 100 only a fraction of failing messages is acted on.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT _dmarc.{domain}` — shows pct below 100.

**How to fix:** Remove the pct tag (defaults to 100) once reports are clean.


### DMARC subdomain policy (sp) weaker than main policy

`email_dmarc_weak_sp` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** Attackers can spoof non-existent subdomains (billing.example.com) if sp=none.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT _dmarc.{domain}` — compare sp= to p=.

**How to fix:** Set `sp=reject` (or remove sp so it inherits p).


### No MTA-STS policy

`email_mtasts_missing` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** MTA-STS forces sending servers to use verified TLS when delivering to you, preventing downgrade/man-in-the-middle on inbound mail.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT _mta-sts.{domain}` and `curl https://mta-sts.{domain}/.well-known/mta-sts.txt`.

**How to fix:** Publish TXT `_mta-sts.<domain>` = `v=STSv1; id=20260101` and host https://mta-sts.&lt;domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt with `version: STSv1`, `mode: enforce`, one `mx:` line per MX host (wildcards allowed), `max_age: 604800`. Use the MX hosts listed in the evidence; for Exchange Online that's `mx: *.mail.protection.outlook.com`. Start with `mode: testing` to confirm nothing breaks.

**References:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/enhancing-mail-flow-with-mta-sts>

### SPF uses deprecated 'ptr' mechanism

`email_spf_ptr` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** `ptr` is slow, unreliable and deprecated; many receivers ignore it.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT {domain}` — look for a `ptr` mechanism.

**How to fix:** Replace `ptr` with explicit ip4/ip6 ranges or includes.


### SPF uses soft-fail (~all)

`email_spf_softfail` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** `~all` is common and acceptable when DMARC is enforced, but `-all` is stronger and tells receivers to reject unlisted senders.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT {domain}` — record ends in `~all`.

**How to fix:** Once all legitimate senders are listed and DMARC reports are clean, change `~all` to `-all`.


### No SMTP TLS reporting (TLS-RPT)

`email_tlsrpt_missing` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** TLS-RPT sends you reports when other servers fail to deliver to you securely.

**How to verify:** `dig +short TXT _smtp._tls.{domain}`.

**How to fix:** TXT `_smtp._tls.<domain>` = `v=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:tlsrpt@<domain>`.


### MTA-STS in testing mode

`email_mtasts_testing` · default severity **info**

**Why it matters:** Policy is published but not enforced.

**How to verify:** `curl https://mta-sts.{domain}/.well-known/mta-sts.txt` — shows mode: testing.

**How to fix:** Switch `mode: testing` to `mode: enforce`.


### DKIM key published

`email_dkim_ok` · passed check (no deduction)


### DMARC enforced

`email_dmarc_ok` · passed check (no deduction)


### MTA-STS enforced

`email_mtasts_ok` · passed check (no deduction)


### SPF record valid and enforcing

`email_spf_ok` · passed check (no deduction)


<a id="dns"></a>

## DNS Health

DNSSEC, CAA, nameserver resilience, zone transfers, subdomain takeover.

### DNS zone transfer (AXFR) allowed to anyone

`dns_axfr_allowed` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** Anyone can download the full zone, revealing every internal hostname.

**How to verify:** `dig AXFR {domain} @<nameserver>` returns the full zone.

**How to fix:** Restrict AXFR to secondary nameserver IPs only (allow-transfer / Zone Transfers tab).


### Dangling CNAME — possible subdomain takeover

`dns_dangling_cname` · default severity **high**

**Why it matters:** This hostname points (CNAME) at a cloud resource that no longer exists. An attacker can often register that resource name and serve content on your subdomain.

**How to verify:** `dig +short CNAME {asset}` then `dig +short A <target>` → NXDOMAIN confirms. Also browse to {asset}: providers show a 'not found / no such app' page. Do NOT attempt to claim the resource yourself. Azure Traffic Manager: `az network traffic-manager profile check-dns --name <name>` is a read-only availability check (nameAvailable: true = claimable).

**How to fix:** Delete the CNAME record, or recreate the resource. For Azure, use domain-verification IDs (asuid TXT) to prevent takeover.

**References:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/security/fundamentals/subdomain-takeover>

### Lame / unresponsive nameserver delegation

`dns_ns_lame` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** A listed nameserver doesn't answer authoritatively for the zone, causing intermittent failures.

**How to verify:** `dig @<nameserver> SOA {domain}` for each NS — look for the `aa` flag in the response.

**How to fix:** Remove the stale NS record at the registrar or fix the zone on that server.


### Fewer than two nameservers

`dns_ns_single` · default severity **medium**

**Why it matters:** A single authoritative nameserver is a single point of failure.

**How to verify:** `dig +short NS {domain}`.

**How to fix:** Use at least two nameservers on separate networks (most DNS providers give 2–4).


### No CAA record

`dns_caa_missing` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** CAA restricts which certificate authorities may issue certificates for the domain.

**How to verify:** `dig +short CAA {domain}`.

**How to fix:** Add CAA records for the CAs you use, e.g. `0 issue "letsencrypt.org"`, `0 issue "digicert.com"`, plus `0 iodef "mailto:security@<domain>"`.


### Stale CNAME — target no longer exists

`dns_dangling_cname_stale` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** This hostname points (CNAME) at a name that no longer resolves. The target has a shape the provider assigns itself (random ID, hash or extra labels), or isn't a known cloud service, so it can't simply be re-registered. It's still a dead record: it breaks the hostname and becomes a takeover if the target name ever becomes available again (for example, an expired domain).

**How to verify:** `dig +short CNAME {asset}` then `dig A <target>` → status NXDOMAIN confirms the record is dead. For a target outside a cloud provider, `whois <target's registered domain>` shows whether that domain has expired (if it has, treat this as a takeover risk).

**How to fix:** Delete the CNAME record (or point it at a live resource). Remove DNS records as part of deprovisioning any cloud resource.

**References:** <https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/security/fundamentals/subdomain-takeover>

### DNSSEC not enabled

`dns_dnssec_missing` · default severity **low**

**Why it matters:** DNSSEC signs DNS answers so resolvers can detect spoofed responses.

**How to verify:** `dig +short DS {domain}` (empty = unsigned) or use dnsviz.net.

**How to fix:** Enable DNSSEC at your DNS host (Cloudflare/Route 53/Azure DNS all support it) and publish the DS record at your registrar.


### CAA record present

`dns_caa_ok` · passed check (no deduction)


### DNSSEC enabled

`dns_dnssec_ok` · passed check (no deduction)


### Nameservers healthy

`dns_ok` · passed check (no deduction)
